newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour plans to shake up monetary policy-making.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour plans to shake up monetary policy-making.

text.p: The main opposition Labour party on Wednesday proposed sweeping changes to the way British interest rates are set with the aim of insulating monetary policy from political manipulation.
Gordon Brown, Labour's economics spokesman, said responsibility for interest rates would remain with the chancellor of the exchequer -- Britain's finance minister.

But he would come to his decisions after taking advice from a broad-based monetary policy committee in the Bank of England (BOE), the central bank, and from a new Council of Economic Advisers within the Treasury.
Brown, whose party is hot favourite to win Britain's looming election, will outline the changes in a speech later today in which he will also set a tough inflation target.

In an interview on BBC radio, Brown said: "I'm not proposing operational independence for the Bank of England in my speech this evening. What I am saying is that we need an interest rate decision-making process that is free from short-term considerations."

Aides said Brown had grown concerned that the monthly meetings between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and BoE governor Eddie George to set interest rates had become too personalised and at times too confrontational.

Brown said monetary policy should be freed from political manipulation and any suspicion that it was being used for party-political ends. Pressed to say whether his ultimate goal was independence for the central bank, Brown said:

"You don't jump to transferring decision-making power until you have looked at both whether you've got the structure properly in place and whether the economic expertise is working effectively and you've got a track record."
"I will look at the situation after we evaluate these two things," he added.
Brown described the changes as some of the biggest since the 1940s and said they would help Britain to escape from the stop-go economic policies that had long bedevilled the country.

The new monetary policy committee -- agreed during private talks with the BOE -- would comprise the governor of the central bank, his deputy, two Bank of England excutive directors and three or four outside figures, Brown's aides said.

The Council of Economic Advisers -- named after the group of economists that advises the U.S. president -- would replace the panel of independent forecasters, or wise men, created to advise the chancellor in the wake of sterling's ejection from the European Exchange Rate mechanism in September 1992.
Brown declined to specify his inflation target but said it would be no softer than Clarke's goal of 2.5 percent or less.

"It will be as tough a target as the Conservatives'. But of course I think we can be tougher in bearing down on inflation by getting the institutional foundations of an anti-inflation policy right," Brown said.

Brown's speech is intended to slot into place the last pieces of the macroeconomic jigsaw that he has assembled recently, notably a commitment to adopt the Conservatives' spending plans for the next two years and to freeze income tax rates for the five-year life of the next parliament.
